A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Now, fresh research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly key role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, fresh research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

It has been revealed that the research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

Recent findings suggest that the latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," states first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an notable effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

It has been revealed that proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

It has been revealed that scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

According to recent reports, to investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she indicates.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In a recent development, in laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Sources indicate that further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

It has been revealed that as a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

Sources indicate that "These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie states. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

Sources indicate that the findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Recent findings suggest that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially key implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Recent findings suggest that arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

According to recent reports, "Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

Industry observers note that the possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence firm AdImpact released Tuesday.
  • Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
  • The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence firm AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, mentioned that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions.".

The record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a fresh high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

It is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

It has been revealed that the fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

  • If all goes according to proposal, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has begun its journey home to Earth.

The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) today at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

If all goes according to proposal, the freighter will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at about 4:55 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). There will be no livestream for its reentry and splashdown. (Today's departure webcast did not feature live footage of the moment of undocking, as it occurred during a gap in coverage of the high-bandwidth signal needed for video.).

The Dragon debuted Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it's the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

In a recent development, the capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It will bring a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

"Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an revision on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “War,” which had its season finale on Nov. 19 on HBO and HBO Max in the U.S., and drops on Nov. 20 on Sky and NOW in the U.K.

Over eight episodes of “War,” actress Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech bro Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) have been squabbling over the couple’s multibillion-dollar fortune as they prepare to part ways for good. The winners, of course, have been the lawyers.

In a recent development, the series centers around two law firms: the modern and fast-paced Taylor & Byrne, founded by Nicholas Taylor (James McArdle) and Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox), and the stuffy, old-school Cathcarts & Sons, led by St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) and Beatrice Ubosi (Nina Sosanya).

In a recent development, if there’s bad blood between Duval and Henderson, relations between the lawyers are worse and bloodier still. Which is perhaps why, in a season finale twist, the divorcing couple decide to negotiate their own settlement amicably, and away from their scheming lawyers.

With Season 1 wrapped up, creator and showrunner George Kay sat down with Variety to talk about some of the real-life inspirations for the show, why he decided on that surprising ending and what we can expect from Season 2, which will see Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts return with a new case and new clients.

According to recent reports, A little bit. Twenty years ago, I had a tech giant that made a documentary series about divorce, and it was quite grim viewing, unsurprisingly. Especially because it was real people, and there was no charisma going on — [“War” director] Ben Taylor wasn’t directing it, basically, and it wasn’t Sienna and Dominic. So I remember having that at the back of my mind, thinking the thing we don’t want here is to make this grim or bleak or anything. And in fact, one of the phrases that we came up with in the writers’ room was that this divorce would be the world’s most expensive couples’ therapy. Even though you don’t physically stay married, you end up closer together.

Recent findings suggest that you want to leave people feeling: “That was good. I liked hanging out with those people.” They were awful a lot of the time, but everyone’s redeemable. And Carla and Morgan don’t despise each other. They just drifted and drifted and drifted.

It has been revealed that I wanted to end that story in Season 1, because I wanted him to find his home. And so that was always intended as a season-long story, and really wrapped around that is that thing of “Is it possible to be a good lawyer and a good person?” And I firmly think it is.

Recent findings suggest that we’re not going to extend the espionage thing. But with Johnny, it’s a question of can you ever trust someone who’s done that? Which I think is a relatable thing, whether that’s your relationship or your workplace. If someone’s done something really untrustworthy, can you ever trust them again? So that will linger, and become a big part of Johnny’s story. But the other thing is, we wanted to find a similar character who’s not at the upper echelons of a law firm to really get behind in Season 2. That is Emma Laird, who plays Molly [a junior lawyer at Taylor & Byrne]. We cast Emma, and I remember saying to her, “You’re amazing. Just so you know, please come and do Molly in Season 1, because there’s loads more coming in Season 2.”.

Every season, I think it’s worth having someone slightly more junior through which to see the whole thing through a prism of them.

It has been revealed that we don’t see her in Season 2. We have guest stars for each season. But we do have a world. So people [in “War”] don’t use X; they use Zephyr. The whole thing keeps kind of bleeding into itself.

That was written with a writer called Toby Finlay, who’s brilliant, and we talked about that a lot in the writers’ room. If you can’t arbitrate on a divorce, you’ll go to litigation, and that’s when it will go public, because it’s not protected anymore. And what’s fun about that is when you’ve got a kind of Morgan Henderson and a Carla Duval, and they are very much in the public eye, that scene triggers the going public of the whole thing. So we were always thinking we want this whole thing to blow up in public on chat demonstrates around “The Milliner,” which is Sienna’s film.

It has been revealed that we wanted to put the camera behind the chat show host and the guest, because it’s only when you go on stage, you suddenly get the on-stage eye-view of what it’s like to be on a chat show. We’re so familiar with Graham Norton or Fallon or whatever, seeing it from the front. We felt it was such a private thing to see it from the other side, and then you can hear the lights kind of cracking in the heat, you see the light obfuscating the audience and the pressure of that. She’s such a talented actress, Sienna. She can do this thing of having a public smile, but with private worry in the eyes.

She was really great in terms of dealing with the script and talking to me about, “I don’t think she’d quite say it like that,” and we would sit there together on set and tweak stuff. But never did we talk about the meta thing of Sienna Miller in the public glare. She was treating it as a proper part.

Industry observers note that “Notting Hill” plays that much more for laughs with Rhys Ifans in his pants. But actually, I felt that [demonstrated] the press physically bearing down on you.

I really wanted to use it as a way to pressurize Sienna, like that door might physically collapse on her. It was a quicker way into just seeing that the weight of the press attention was right there, so it’s a little nod to “Notting Hill,” just in the sheer kind of [gasp] of opening the door. But it’s not used for laughs.

Industry observers note that who was the guy that chased that woman down the corridor? It was awful.

I think it’s more that sort of stuff happens in hotels, and there’s CCTV in hotels. You’re always looking in thrillers to find ways you could kind of revisit. So it wasn’t trying to plug into any one particular incident.

In a recent development, I wanted to make it a bit different because — full disclosure — I didn’t want Olivia Wilde to think we were just aping her experience. But also, I thought by distancing ourselves from it, we could make it even worse for Carla by putting it right in her biggest night, her biggest moment. This really is the culmination. She’s on a career comeback at that point. She’s been in some less good movies than “The Milliner,” if you can imagine, and so this was a really special night for her. So using that for dramatic effect felt good.

But the thing that I was really inspired by the Olivia Wilde thing was just how professional and upset she was at the same time. Like we’re talking about Sienna’s ability to [show] the pain it’s caused, and then you see how she’s painting on a smile promptly to get through it. And I really spotted that in Olivia Wilde’s way of dealing with that in that moment, which I thought that just reflected very well on Olivia Wilde. So I was happy to be inspired by that because it’s probably an awful moment in someone’s life, and you’ve got to be choose the right way to kind of be inspired.

There were lots of fun names. The script editor came up with a brilliant list of films that are sort of mid-level Euro, kind of awards worthy, like “The Red Violinist of Marseille” and things like that, or you know, “The Harpist of Madrid.” But in the end, it was just “The Milliner.” We had this story that she was undercover in occupied Europe with a hat.

It has been revealed that the thing we look for in the divorce [case] is to analyze the relationships of all the lawyers. And with the libel case, it’s all about reputation. How our reputations are affecting us at work and what our work reputation means to us in life is a really cool thing to have exposed by a libel trial. So it’s about playing those two things off against each other, and bringing in a few latest characters and a few new bits of casting to make it believable that what we see as predominantly family lawyers can also have other people in their departments who have libel experience.

Industry observers note that nick Mohammed really comes through in Season 2, which was again part of our pledge to him. And there’s a fresh hiring at Cathcarts, who starts to — not cause problems, but definitely shakes up the dynamic.

It has been revealed that tonally, it’s adjacent but it’s not exactly the same. And we want to have different aspects. It’s a different album.

Recent findings suggest that I’m actually looking the other way. I’m looking for the thing that affects people and then looking for the legal equivalent. It’s the relationship stories that we’ve seen in movies or in our own lives that we really relate to on an emotional level, and then quickly scouring law to say, “Well, where is that felt?” So it’s less with Walliams or Russell Brand. Like, I’m interested in how the justice system will treat those people, but I’m not using that for inspiration for drama because I don’t know how it feels for anyone involved because I don’t know it. So we’re trying to start with the feeling.

A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for newly introduced treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • Sources indicate that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for newly introduced treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

Sources indicate that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Sources indicate that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Industry observers note that most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Sources indicate that over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Sources indicate that despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

Industry observers note that to investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

As the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

The researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

To understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

It has been revealed that the researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

In a recent development, additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

Industry observers note that A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially key targets for future drugs.

However, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

Newly introduced Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

Recent findings suggest that "For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly key for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

In a recent development, dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential latest therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

Sources indicate that "We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for newly introduced treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

It has been revealed that dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, noted:.

"This research highlights how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing fresh knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

#13161. Tech Report: “The Secrecy Was Insane:” The Making of ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ From Locked Safes to Original Cast’s Return

Tech Report: “The Secrecy Was Insane:” The Making of ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ From Locked Safes to Original Cast’s Return

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hollywoodreporter

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that some stories refuse to stay on the page.
  • Before the odds could be in their favor, the creative team behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had to survive a Games of their own, one played entirely in secret.
  • Industry observers note that the rules were simple: one copy of the book, no internet and not a word to anyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that some stories refuse to stay on the page. The Hollywood Reporter’s Beyond the Book column explores what happens when books make the leap to screen and beyond — unpacking what stayed, changed, how it was done and why it matters with the creatives who made it.

Before the odds could be in their favor, the creative team behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping had to survive a Games of their own, one played entirely in secret.

Industry observers note that the rules were simple: one copy of the book, no internet and not a word to anyone. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Hunts Down $21M in Box Office Previews Movies Jennifer Lawrence Thinks Her 'Hunger Games' Bow and Arrow Prop Was Stolen.

When Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins called her trusted adapters, director Francis Lawrence, producer Nina Jacobson and original Hunger Games screenwriter Billy Ray, they were eager to read her new story. The catch: it wasn’t fully finished, and it hadn’t been announced to the public. That meant caution was essential.

In a recent development, take Ray’s process for example. The screenwriter didn’t write his latest Hunger Games script on his own computer. Each day, he drove onto the Fox lot to Jacobson’s office and sat down in a small room with a safe that guarded Collins’ story. An assistant opened the safe, took out a laptop that had never been connected to the internet and set it in front of him. He wrote all day, stated “Done,” and the laptop went back into the safe.

“That’s how the script got written, which of course I had never done before,” Ray tells The Hollywood Reporter.

It was an unusual way to adapt a novel that almost no one outside that small circle knew existed, yet maintaining strict confidentiality was imperative given the phenomenon Collins’ franchise has become. The original four films — The Hunger Games, Catching Fire and Mockingjay Part 1 and 2 — grossed roughly $2.98 billion worldwide. Debuting with its first book in 2008, the dystopian saga following teenagers forced into fatal combat has grown into one of the most successful young adult publishing franchises in history. Across its five installments, the series has sold more than 100 million copies globally.

Sources indicate that in 2020, Collins released her first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, which chronicled the rise of the tyrant Coriolanus Snow. The film was adapted for feature film starring Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler. Now with Sunrise on the Reaping, released on Nov. 20, Collins has returned to another familiar face: Haymitch Abernathy, the District 12 mentor Woody Harrelson played in the films.

It has been revealed that the prequel revisits the world of Panem 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games, starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, when a younger Haymitch (portrayed by Joseph Zada) competes. Sunrise on the Reaping opens on Haymitch’s 16th birthday, which coincides with the second Quarter Quell, where the traditional choice of one male and one female from a district has been doubled to two of each.

Though initially not among the four selected tributes for District 12, Haymitch is automatically volunteered as punishment for trying to protect his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) who reacts after one of the chosen boys tries to make a run for it and is shot by Capitol soldiers known as “Peacekeepers.”.

The Haymitch origin story answers a question fans have had since the first film: how the hopeful, mischievous kid became the bitter, drunken mentor to Jennifer Lawrence‘s Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson‘s Peeta Mellark that Harrelson played.

Ahead of the film’s release, Ray, Jacobson and director Francis Lawrence spoke with THR about working under an NDA bubble, finding their newly introduced Haymitch and reuniting franchise alums Harrelson, Lawrence and Hutcherson.

When The Hunger Games was first adapted for the screen, screenwriter Ray and director Gary Ross launched what would grow into a global success. Since both Ray and Ross parted ways with the franchise following the initial installment, Ray’s comeback to craft the backstory for a character he helped popularize represented a complete full-circle experience.

“Having debuted that franchise, The Hunger Games has been such a blessing in my career,” Ray tells THR. “I can’t begin to enumerate all the ways it’s been great for me.”.

“When the opportunity came to come back, I remarked yes before I read the book,” he says of his return. “It was something I wanted to do. I wanted to work with Francis, and I wanted to be back under the hood with Suzanne and with Nina.”.

Sources indicate that ray has stayed close with Collins, who read an early draft of his debut novel, Burn the Water, which was released earlier this year. “It was as if we had spoken the day before,” he says of reteaming with Collins and others for Sunrise on the Reaping. “There was just no falloff at all.”.

According to recent reports, when Collins calls, producer Jacobson, director Lawrence and Ray answer, ready to find out what the author has created this time. But her first question is always the same: “Why don’t you guys take a look and let me know if you think it’s a movie?”.

“This is always kind of hilarious… We read this one and said, ‘Yeah, it’s a movie, Suzanne,'” Lawrence says, laughing. Jacobson’s answer was just as immediate: “My first response was, ‘Hell yes.'”.

Collins’ question is a sincere one, though, Lawrence explains. “She’s very serious when she states it’s OK to tell her it’s not a movie. When you create anything, you’re vulnerable, and when she hands something to us, it’s usually not completely finished. She feels vulnerable about it and wants some reassurance that it really is worthy of being on the screen.”.

Getting that far took some doing. When the team read an early draft of The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, the world was in lockdown, so keeping it secret was easier, Lawrence claims. Sunrise on the Reaping brought “a different kind of tension, because the book had not yet been published, so the secrecy and security around the project was pretty extreme,” Ray says.

Recent findings suggest that “For us, the secrecy was insane,” Jacobson claims. “We had one hard copy of the book. It had to be mailed or messengered from Latest York to L.A. in sections. First it lived at her [Collins’] agent’s house and then eventually we got a safe for my office and it moved into the safe. There was one copy, and people could make an appointment if they needed to read it.”.

It has been revealed that the secrecy extended to casting, too. “Even once we had our script, we couldn’t release sides, or even use a scene from the book instead of sides, because if we read an actor, people would know what scenes and characters were in the book besides Haymitch,” Jacobson says. “So we had the young actors do improvs, just so we could get acquainted with this generation of actors and start to collect knowledge about who they are.”.

“Having to keep it locked down in this NDA bubble was exciting,” she adds. “It was sort of stressful, and I was incredibly relieved when we could finally talk about it!”.

“We knew Haymitch was going to be the trickiest person to cast, because we’re anchored with him,” Lawrence claims.

Joseph Zada, who starred in Prime Video’s We Were Liars and had filmed Netflix’s East of Eden series, caught the attention of casting directors Debra Zane and Dylan Jury, who wanted Lawrence and Jacobson to meet him.

In a recent development, “He had sent in an improv tape. We had many, many people do improv tapes just to see who was out in the world, and his was pretty special,” Lawrence recalls.

From there, the audition process became its own Hunger Games. “We really put him through the wringer in the audition process,” the director admits. “We tested and tested to make sure he would be emotionally capable of going through everything he needed to go through, that he had the sense of mischief and irreverence Woody has, and that he could embody all those characteristics without feeling like he was doing an impression. That was the tricky thing. But he was definitely the guy.”.

“We needed to know he had the range to experience all of the loss in the movie, and to do it in different ways: sometimes shame, guilt or anger, or just complete loss and grief,” Lawrence adds. “We needed somebody who could bring all of that.”.

Industry observers note that for Jacobson, the deciding quality was mischief. “You needed somebody who had mischief in them, and that’s a surprisingly hard thing to find,” she says. “There are some wonderful, likable actors who are very capable leading men, but who don’t necessarily have that mischief in them, that troublemaker vibe. And yet at his young age, it can’t be that dark, twisted kind of mischief-maker or trickster. It’s a boyish quality.”.

Zada was someone who “had a hopeful, sunny disposition” and the mischief they wanted Haymitch to embody.

According to recent reports, “When you first meet him in the original movies, you don’t understand why he’s so angry, drunken, broken and bitter. You assume, well, it can’t be easy being a mentor for the poorest, most disadvantaged district out there,” she continues. “What all of us wanted to see in this one, and what Joseph captured so beautifully, is that he was bright, funny, hopeful and very apolitical.”.

Zada’s chemistry with Peak, cast as his love interest, Lenore Dove, sealed it. “You just felt it. You felt like this woman is the woman he loves. She’s his best friend. She’s the person who makes it all make sense for him,” Jacobson indicates of their chemistry reads together.

“There’s a quality about Woody, and we had to find someone who had that quality but wasn’t going to get burdened by it,” she notes. “With all of our actors, we always noted, ‘We don’t want impersonation. We want interpretation.'”.

That philosophy extended well beyond Haymitch. From Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning to Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons and Ralph Fiennes, Sunrise wasn’t short on A-listers joining its younger, newer cast members that also included Mckenna Grace, Ben Wang, Molly McCann and Percy Daggs IV.

Recent findings suggest that but joining an established franchise isn’t always an immediate yes, Jacobson indicates. “There are definitely some people who just don’t know the series that well, so it’s about educating them about it, and making sure they know we’re not looking for them to impersonate,” she explains. “We want their interpretation of the character. If they don’t know the series, oftentimes they have to go ask around a bit and talk to people in their lives.”.

Culkin and Fanning, who play Caesar Flickerman and Effie Trinket, have been candid about finding their own interpretations while respecting the characters Stanley Tucci and Elizabeth Banks originated.

“What we tell people who are new to it, and I really do believe this quite earnestly, is that it’s one of the very few franchises where, for each of the renowned actors we cast, it is actually all about performance. It’s never about prosthetics or visual effects,” Jacobson indicates. (Well, almost never: “Of course we use those things sparingly here and there. Those are not Glenn’s teeth,” she notes.).

In a recent development, the appeal, she states, is the creative freedom that comes with everything being “rooted in performance.” “You’re going to be collaborating closely with Francis and the department heads on the creation, building and design of your character, and it’s going to come down to meaty character work. You’re very rarely against a green screen. You’re almost always in a practical location with, hopefully, some other amazing actors in the scenes with you. I think these movies give each actor a real showcase of their talents, in a way that isn’t always true in a lot of other franchises.”.

Jacobson recalls Sunrise on the Reaping being an “incredibly emotional” read. “I cried quite a few times, and then cried quite a lot at the end. I found it so fully moving and satisfying on so many levels.”.

But how do you adapt a book fans haven’t been able to read yet? The creative team relied on being fans themselves.

Sources indicate that “Nina and I consider ourselves fans, so there are a lot of things we fight to keep from the book, details we love ourselves,” Lawrence claims. “And Suzanne is obviously going to fight for certain things: making sure her themes, ideas, the spirit of the characters and their emotional arcs are there. So there’s a good group of us there to protect what we think fans are going to love.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The funny thing is, it’s incredibly easy for me to know how fans will feel, because I’m the OG fan,” Jacobson says. “I’m as obsessed with the books as any diehard fan, and so is Francis.”.

Sources indicate that still, some things had to go. “If I put everything that’s in the book into the movie, the movie would be six hours long. You can’t do that,” Ray says.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise doubles the number of tributes competing in the Games, and the team knew they couldn’t explore every one in depth. “Getting to know the tributes and understanding potential allies and enemies is one of the parts of these movies people really enjoy and are invested in. So figuring out how to balance the 48, and making sure we gave time and attention to the core characters whose stories are connected to Haymitch’s journey, was a definite challenge,” Jacobson claims.

The book is also told entirely from Haymitch’s point of view, which posed its own challenge. “What we found even in the original movies with Katniss was that if she wasn’t in a scene, the scene still needed to be about her in some way,” Jacobson indicates. “But when you’re only ever with that one person, there’s notable context and opportunities you might miss. So figuring out where to break with his point of view, when to show something he can’t see or know, was a massive decision in the adaptation process.”.

As for every other decision, the guiding principle was Collins.

“At the very beginning of the process, I asked Suzanne, ‘What is this book about for you?'” Ray recalls. “She talked about the philosophy of the book: the philosophy of propaganda and implicit submission, the philosophy of Thomas Hobbes, David Hume and John Locke. And I said, ‘Suzanne, what’s the book about for you emotionally?’ She said, ‘It’s about love and loss.’ I said, ‘Great, that’s what I’m writing.’ So anything that didn’t stick to that had to go.”.

The Haymitch audiences meet in Sunrise is a far cry from the broken alcoholic of the original films. In Sunrise, audiences encounter a teen initially easygoing and unconcerned with politics. But his life transforms when he is forced into the 50th Hunger Games. Refusing to simply comply, he attempts to disrupt the Capitol’s system and oppose President Snow, altering both his own destiny and the world around him.

Jacobson likens the young Haymitch to the “kind of guy who’s probably not very serious about school and is just waiting for the end of the day to run down to the beach with his surfboard and his girlfriend, hang out and catch some waves.” His attitude, as she sees it: “I can’t do anything about this broken world that I live in, but I’ve got a girl I love and a family I love, and that’s enough for me. Who am I? What difference would I make anyway?”.

Sources indicate that jacobson sees Haymitch’s arc as similar to Katniss’, with a priority on family that grows to include their community and district. “Your circle of concern grows in each movie, and there’s a cost to expanding that circle, a price to pay… But it’s the things he hears and brings with him from Lenore Dove. He says the Capitol has all the power and always will, and she says that doesn’t mean they always have, and it doesn’t mean they always will. It’s this notion that it’s not a foregone conclusion that oppressive power structures can’t be disrupted and ultimately destroyed.”.

In a recent development, the Haymitch of the film faces a dilemma: “What am I willing to give up for the people I care about? And what am I willing to give up to right these really profound wrongs and try to end the Games?”.

“Seeing him get radicalized, and seeing him decide, even with all this loss, that the way to honor these people is to continue to fight: that was what was really important to me, and what I found really interesting and moving,” Lawrence claims.

“You see Haymitch in the other movies, and Woody does an amazing job portraying him, but people laugh with him,” the director adds. “He’s a drunk, and you just don’t know the history. Now you follow this movie and see all that he went through, how long and hard he fought, all the years he had to escort tributes to the arena and watch them die. But he continued to fight and kept his promise to his girlfriend, his mother, his brother, to Maysilee (portrayed by Grace) and all of them.”.

For Ray, filling in that history was the point. “In that first movie, obviously Haymitch is just broken, with a real serious drinking problem and a lot of pain. This was the movie that explained all that, and it was great to do that sort of history retroactively, to say, ‘This explains the behavior you’ve been seeing through all those movies,'” he says. “People know what happened, and the trick is saying, ‘Here’s the part you didn’t know.’ That’s what we were going for here.”.

In a recent development, collins doesn’t write unless she has something to say, and themes have been the foundation of each Hunger Games book. With the original trilogy, she explored the consequences of war for teens. With the prequels, she continues to examine the state of the world.

It has been revealed that “Look at the themes she’s dealing with now and how relevant they are: there’s a bit of a call to action, this idea of implicit submission, and diving into the use of propaganda to get people to submit. So there are fresh ideas that feel very relevant. There’s meat on the bone,” Lawrence says. “Take this idea of implicit submission. You can look at any government, whether it’s authoritarian, fascist or one that calls itself democratic: as humans, we always agree to be ruled by the few. It’s a bit of a call to action: don’t be apathetic, stand up, voice your beliefs, and don’t expect instant gratification, because change may take time. I feel that’s very relevant now, but it’s also timeless, because people are constantly fighting for their rights. You see it in Hungary, with the ousting of a regime, and in Brazil, where people actually make change. That’s happening now, but it’s also something that’s been happening for thousands of years.”.

Ray says he approached both the original film and Sunrise as if they were “true stories.”.

According to recent reports, “And they’re getting closer and closer to being that, which is the bad news for us as a culture, and the great news for Suzanne Collins, because she has her finger on the pulse of something, and it does feel like a true story. If you think of it that way, you can write it as a screenwriter from a place of complete outrage,” he claims.

Haymitch’s journey matters now even more given it’s “a time when so many people feel like, ‘What’s the point of trying to make a difference?'” Jacobson says. “It’s a story that is so emotional about how hard it is to try to make a difference. It’s also about how what you set in motion today might not be realized for another generation, and how hard it is to continue to resist and to endure, knowing that the changes you hope for could take 25 years to accomplish.”.

Anyone who knows The Hunger Games knows the brutality of the story. “I think an audience that has bought into the concept that a government forces children to kill each other knows they’re coming to see something dark,” Ray says. “I don’t think anybody is going to come away saying, ‘Wow, I was expecting a musical. What the hell is this?'”.

Even so, certain sequences in Sunrise had to be toned down to keep the film’s PG-13 rating.

“There’s a moment in the book where a character is holding the head of a child, and I thought, ‘We’re never going to be able to do that.’ There were probably three moments in the book where I went, ‘Come on, Suzanne, this is never going to happen.’ And she understands that when we get into the process,” Lawrence states.

The story’s emotional darkness stayed intact, and Lawrence says it was “toughest” on Zada, who had to ride that roller coaster on set.

“Whenever we led up to certain days, whether it was a Lenore Dove scene or a Maysilee scene, it was always a little scary for him, because he knew he’d have to sit in those feelings for 10 or 12 hours, basically all day,” he indicates.

The Games were filmed first, with the District 12 scenes shot later. “He was so happy to just be happy: going to work convinced he’d never get called in the reaping, having a nice scene in the meadow with Lenore Dove, being in the candy shop. He looked forward to those days,” Lawrence indicates.

But the darker turns were never far off. “We also had to do things like shoot his and Lenore Dove’s first scene one day and then, because we were in that location, jump to the end the very next day and do that whole scene (readers know the one.) That was tough on Joe. Even when he was happy to be happy, he knew what was coming tomorrow. That weighed on him more than it did on me,” the director says.

Recent findings suggest that though the book and film follow a younger Haymitch, the book’s epilogue, featuring Katniss, Peeta and an older Haymitch, was in the script from the start. “It was such a profound honor to get to write those characters again. It was just pure joy,” Ray claims.

“I remember reading the epilogue in the manuscript and thinking, ‘Wow, this is fantastic.’ I found it really moving,” Lawrence notes of the trio’s return in the book.

In a recent development, “The hope was always to bring them back,” the director states of Harrelson, Hutcherson and Jennifer Lawrence. But because of the secrecy surrounding the book and the adaptation, “We didn’t reach out to them until, I want to say, the day before the announcement. That’s when I called the three of them.”.

While the team hoped for an immediate yes, they prepared in case scheduling conflicts or other circumstances kept the actors from returning. “We had already tasked ourselves with figuring out how to make the story as fulfilling as possible if it didn’t happen,” Lawrence says.

But there was no need to rethink the epilogue: the actors were “all very excited to return,” he notes. “Then it was really just a scheduling question: when can we get the three of them together and out to Germany?” the director says.

In a recent development, francis Lawrence has stayed in touch with the cast, but working together again in the world of The Hunger Games made for an especially meaningful reunion. “I think it was a Wednesday night when they arrived, and I got a text from Jen that she and Josh were having a beer in the hotel bar. I was coming back from set, so I joined, then Nina joined, and our cinematographer, the still photographer, the sound mixer… It’s the same group of people who have been making these movies for 16 years, so we had this great reunion of about 30 of us before costume fittings and all of that.”.

Industry observers note that with two prequel novels and films now out, the question is always whether there are more stories to tell in Panem. The creative team admits they’re just as in the dark as everyone else.

“She only really writes when she has something to say, so I hope she has something she wants to write about in this world, because I would miss it a lot,” Jacobson indicates.

It has been revealed that fans have been quick to name the characters they’d love to follow in their early years, with Finnick (portrayed by Sam Claflin) and Johanna (Jena Malone) at the top of the list, along with the first Hunger Games. After Sunrise, Jacobson’s own fascination is Plutarch. “When I realized from this book that Plutarch has been playing a double agent for 25 years by the time you meet him in Catching Fire, that to me is pretty fascinating. How do you pull that off? How could you possibly live that close to such danger? And what compromises did you have to make? He is not a morally clean character at all, so I have a total fascination with him,” she claims.

If the prequels have proved anything, it’s to never say never, a lesson Jacobson notes the team learned early. “When we finished the original trilogy of books, we really thought we were done. We’ve never tried to make a movie without a book of hers. We only make her books. We never tried to develop anything that wasn’t based on something she had given us as a book she was going to publish. So when we first got Ballad, all of a sudden it was, ‘Oh my god, we’re coming back to this world.'”.

Sources indicate that “I was so wowed by the way she’s taken us on this journey, and by the amount of things that come together in this movie from all of the books and all of the movies. On the other hand, honestly, you could make this [Sunrise] the first book you’ve ever read, or the first movie you’ve seen. You could start here, make it your jumping-off point, and then go in any order you wanted. So there’s accessibility for everyone.”.

As for future stories, Lawrence and Jacobson are hopeful but note only Collins will know the answer.

“I don’t know if ‘superstitious’ is the right word, but she really does not let on whether or not she’s writing,” Lawrence says of Collins. “If she gets an idea and works on it, she keeps quiet, then turns it in to her publisher, who she trusts immensely, and waits to hear that it’s a publishable book. Only then does she tell us she’s written something.”.

Industry observers note that “I have not heard anything. Would I love her to write another book? Yes, I sure would, because I still love the world so much, and I still find there’s so much to learn,” Jacobson says. “Because she digs so deep in terms of both history and philosophy, I hope she still has so much more to say, and I hope she’ll decide to say it in Panem. But I don’t know. We haven’t gotten any winks or nods yet. I hope I get a wink and a nod, but I have gotten no winks, no nods so far.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Sources indicate that climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In a recent development, in the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

According to recent reports, while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar stated. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that at the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute mentioned it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky glitch. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar remarked. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

Industry observers note that "You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar mentioned, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar mentioned, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

In a recent development, carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

In a recent development, "Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Recent findings suggest that carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".
